newsitem.title: FINLAND: NEW FINNISH CURRENCY ACT BILL TO PARL SPRING '98.
newsitem.headline: NEW FINNISH CURRENCY ACT BILL TO PARL SPRING '98.

text.p: The government will give in spring 1998 to parliament a new proposal to revise the Finnish Currency Act, aiming to scrap by end-1998 the exchange rate policy influence now wielded by the central bank's supervisory board, a senior finance ministry official said on Tuesday.
The government had intended to strip the board of parliamentary supervisors of that authority already from the start of 1998, but ran into stiff opposition in the assembly.

Delivering its response to a government proposal to reform outdated central bank legislation, including a change in the currency act, parliament's economic committee in a statement received on Tuesday rejected the proposed currency act bill.

"We can live with that," cabinet counselor Pekka Laajanen at the finance ministry told Reuters by telephone. "It simply means that the currency act will take effect one year later than planned. A new proposal will be given next spring," he said.
"The supervisory board's authority in decision-making on the external value of the markka would so remain intact," the economic committee said.

The board's role in decisions regarding the external value of the markka is to approve or reject changes proposed by the Bank of Finland's board of management, and to forward the changes proposed by the board of management to the government, which makes the final decision.
Neither the supervisory board nor the government may on their own alter the board of management's proposal.

If Finland decides to join EMU in 1999 -- parliament is due to vote on membership early next year -- and if the EU approves Finnish entry (Finland meets all convergence criteria), the board of parliamentary supervisors will have a say on the exchange rate at which the markka will be irrevocably fixed to the new euro currency in 1999.

They would also be called upon to participate in Finland's formal national decisions on the exchange rates at which any potential new members of Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) would be admitted.
